input.question: How do business with open wifi not get in trouble when their customers download protected content?
input.ground_truth: The RIAA doesn't typically go after people downloading a single song. They go after people that they identify (sometimes wrongly) as sharing songs so other can download them. It has generally been show that the RIAA's tactics are more for the publicity that actually stopping file sharing. They are more than willing to settle out of court for ridiculous fees (to an individual) than complete the prosecution. If they seriously went after a business like Starbucks then they would have to compete with Starbuck's deep pockets and armies of lawyers, and they might loose. That looks really bad and is not what they want to do.

Okay! Imagine you have a lemonade stand. Lots of people come to your stand and you let them sit on your bench and use your phone’s internet (that’s like having open wifi).

Now, imagine one of your friends sits on your bench and uses your phone’s internet to watch a movie that they’re not supposed to watch. The movie company says, “Hey! That’s not allowed!”

But here’s the thing: you didn’t tell your friend to watch the movie. You just let them use your phone’s internet. It’s like letting someone use your sidewalk to walk by – you can’t control what they do once they’re walking.

The law usually says that the person who actually downloads the movie is the one who did something wrong, not the person who just let them use the internet. So, the lemonade stand (the business) usually doesn’t get in trouble just for letting people use their wifi, as long as they didn’t tell them to do something wrong.

But, sometimes, if the business knows someone is doing something really bad and they don’t stop them, they might get in trouble. But just letting people use the wifi? Usually, that’s okay.
